ratings.excerpt: Sean Hayes gives an astonishing performance … Will and Grace’s Sean Hayes stars as trouble pianist Oscar Levant in a fast-paced, zinger-packed play which has an unforgettable climax … Sean Hayes, best known as the bitchily bright-eyed Jack McFarland in sitcom Will and Grace, transforms himself here into Oscar Levant … Doug Wright’s play is a fast-paced, highly polished, zinger-packed vehicle for his astonishing performance, which culminates in an electrifyingly expressive live rendition of Rhapsody in Blue … Sure, the play is schematic in its discussion of genius and madness and the boundaries of taste in television, and in the way it tees up one-liners for Oscar to thwack home. … ... everyone else on stage is a mere feed for Oscar and the show is built around Hayes’s performance. … The de

Sean Hayes on dazzling form … The Will & Grace star delivers a fantastically energised performance as the troubled musician Oscar Levant in this fine Broadway import … What sets this dazzling, considered Tony award-winning Broadway transfer apart is the fantastically energised performance from Sean Hayes … The director Lisa Peterson snaps sure-footedly through the action, while allowing the tender moments to breathe.

Sean Hayes and Rosalie Craig shine in the transfer of this Tony-winning play about a pianist disintegrating on a ’50s talk show … Focused so tightly on the early days of American TV, this could potentially sound niche for a British audience. But in Wright’s assured hands, the collision of Levant’s private and public life down the barrel of a camera lens becomes a play about the beginning of so many things we now recognise as staples of celebrity culture. … Hayes is extraordinary as Levant, crumpling into himself even as he makes the one-liners prompted by Parr sing off the stage. His well-honed way with comedy is the play’s secret weapon. … There’s a grippingly feverish quality to how Rachel Huack’s dressing room and studio sets end up sharing stage space. … It's fragmentary and frantic –

Sean Hayes is flawless in his West End debut … Anybody who only knows Sean Hayes from his beloved turn as sassy, über-gay Jack in long-running US sitcom Will & Grace... is in for a revelation when they see his Tony-winning performance in this Broadway import. He’s barely recognisable. … Doug Wright’s play, running at a snappy, high-stakes, interval-free 100 minutes … Wright’s script is very funny indeed, interpolating outrageous real-life quotes from Levant (“schizophrenia: it beats dining alone … underneath this flabby exterior is an enormous lack of character … Hayes inhabits his role so completely and with such detail that he’s equal parts mesmerising and painful to watch. … All of the acting is first-rate. Sean Hayes’ powerful, committed central performance holds together this story of a musical genius unravelling live on air … Wright’s writing can feel overwrought in places, cranking up the interpersonal drama with predictable, mechanical regularity like a metronome. But the script is at its best where Wright simply lets Levant speak for himself, rolling out a slew of his most quotably snarky remarks. … Director Lisa Peterson gives the production a slick, effective staging, conveying both the exhilarating momentum and crushing time pressure of a live broadcast … Heading an uneven cast, Sean Hayes gives a consummate, larger-than-life performance as Oscar, channelling a profoundly unsettled, manic energy … ... Sean Hayes brings panache to tense talkshow encounter … Will & Grace star reprises his Tony award-winning role as Oscar Levant in Doug Wright’s play about a ratings-crucial TV interview … ... in a play that explicitly hymns integrity and honesty in the entertainment industry, it feels queasy that the events depicted in Good Night, Oscar never occurred as shown. … As Levant, Hayes gives a performance of such busyness – twitches, tics, lip curls, cigarette business – that you wonder if the stage has a fast-forward button. Sean Hayes hits the right notes in quippy pianist bio-drama … Mental health and the ghost of Gershwin loom large in Doug Wright’s Tony-winning play about the darkly witty Oscar Levant … ... as the play shifts from faction to expressionist psychodrama it feels as if Wright and director Lisa Peterson can’t decide where they want to take us. … There are rather lukewarm parentheses on comedy’s duty to say the unsayable, tantalising moments of tenderness between Levant and his wife (Craig bringing emotional hurt to a script heavy on flashy quips) and hints of a deeper exploration of mental health. … But that’s all blown away by one coup de théâtre... Hayes on a Steinway is the real deal — and it’s worth the wait.

Tony-winning Sean Hayes exudes awkward brilliance and pathos as a troubled pianist … Doug Wright’s midcentury period piece delivers a glimmering, beguiling surface without looking too hard at what’s going on underneath … In a Tony Award-winning performance, its star Sean Hayes (Will & Grace) drenches this role in pathos and awkward brilliance, his sharp edges and jagged nerves rubbing uncomfortably against the smooth patter of a 1958 episode of Tonight Starring Jimmy Paar. … Playwright Doug Wright is clearly captivated by his subject, but UK audiences might not be too familiar with Levant … As Wright’s play emphasises, Levant’s worldview was ahead of its time – and so were the people who hired him... Good Night, Oscar is a Tony Award winner, but nobody this side of the Atlantic will care … Doug Wright has serious points to make but it’s a tricky proposition in Britain … ... we leave this 100-minute play no wiser as to the real man behind this troubled facade.
